newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Watching and waiting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Watching and waiting.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market will have little to do on Wednesday, but to watch and wait for key data due on Friday and next week, analysts said.

"I suspect that what will happen tomorrow and Thursday is, number one, it will be rather dull, and number two, the market's probably going to be very focused on Friday's numbers," said Elliott Platt, managing director, economic research, at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
On Friday, the government will report September retail sales and the September Producer Price Index (PPI).
The only economic data the market will get on Wednesday are August wholesale inventories. In July, those inventories rose a slight 0.1 percent.

"August wholesale inventories won't cause any market reaction, but they are interesting because at all stages of processing, inventories look low relative to sales," said Dana Johnson, head of research for First Chicago Capital Markets.
"If that pattern continues, there's not much likelihood of the economy getting weak on us," Johnson said.
Platt said that, over the next couple of days, market chatter about upcoming data could increase.
The chatter could focus on potential revisions to previously reported data, especially retail sales data.
"There is a history of upward revisions to August retail sales and we think it's very possible that will happen this year, too," said Platt.

As for the PPI due on Friday, economists surveyed by Reuters offered an average forecast of a 0.3 percent rise, or a 0.2 percent gain in the core PPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components. If the PPI comes in as expected, or slightly more subdued than anticipated, the market could do a little better, Platt said.
But upside will be limited because the market will already have its eye the September Consumer Price Index (CPI) due on Wednesday, October 16, analysts said.
"More and more the CPI report is shaping up as the big hurdle fot his market," said Johnson.
Meanwhile, the market will work on consolidating the gains of the rally of the last couple of weeks, Johnson said.
"The traders are very much aware of the market's pattern of moving to the extreme right after the monthly employment report and then backtracking for the rest of the month," said Johnson.
"People are a little afraid of that pattern repeating itself," he said.

"We're in this range of 6.75 percent to seven percent (on the 30-year Treasury bond yield) and clearly, the market has difficulty getting through the 6.75 percent barrier with any conviction," said Platt.
In late afternoon trade on Tuesday, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was down 5/32 to 99-11/32, yielding 6.80 percent.
Dealers expected Federal funds to open between 5-5/16 percent and 5-3/8 percent on Wednesday.
